newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - What's in NZ's post-election grab bag?.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - What's in NZ's post-election grab bag?.

text.p: By Adrian Orr, Chief Economist, National Bank of NZ Ltd.
WELLINGTON - The people have spoken and the pollsters were right. Winston Peters (NZ First) holds the "balance of responsibility" in the political arena.

National gained 44 seats, with its allies (ACT and United) a further 9. Their rivals, Labour and Alliance, secured 37 and 13 seats respectively. This should be declared a victory to the centre-right vote, but for the vagaries of MMP.
Instead, things are on hold in anticipation of NZ First's majority-forming decision about what to do with their 17 seats.
Their immediate response? Go fishing, literally.

A big clue as to which side of the fence NZ First may fall is their capture of all five Maori electorate seats. This implies a labour-leaning NZ First caucus, despite the more natural National-leaning of their leader.
However, since the election Tau Henare, NZ First's second in command, has offered an olive branch to the National Party.

Is this an attempt to raise Labour's offerings? Something to placate financial markets for the interim? Or, a sop to the boss himself? If it's the latter then many Maori voters may soon feel betrayed. However, don't hold your breath waiting for a decision, this could take weeks.

With everyone courting NZ First, what's up for grabs on the policy platter? Judging from the early embraces, most things excluding Alliance's and ACT's offerings. These parties form the outer boundaries for the left and right respectively, and will play more minor broking roles.
Before going through possible coalition agreements, an English lesson is timely.
"Non-negotiable" in MMP terms means "don't mention it" to the coalition partner. This falls short of the Concise Oxford Dictionary definition, but highlights the marvel of MMP.
Shared policies can be got on with, while disagreements can be swept aside in a political face-saving fashion.
Now let's consider a Labour-NZ First coalition deal.
The "non-negotiable" policies from NZ First will likely include: the buy-back of forests, fair trade tariffs, foreign ownership restrictions of strategic assets, and compulsory retirement saving.
These can all be tabled in parliament outside a coalition deal, with NZ First's full confidence that they will be rejected.

Labour, by contrast, were more miserly with their pre-election promises and will go into bat on most. The batting order will include: the Reserve Bank Act and inflation targets, fiscal expenditure and debt targets, taxation policy, the Employment Contracts Act, and social policy.
First, monetary policy.

NZ First would likely be appeased with a widening of the inflation target range (i.e. -1.0 percent to 3.0 percent) and a full review of the consumer price index. It is unlikely that they would hold out for the inclusion of specific Reserve Bank growth targets or a shift to an average trading partner inflation target.
Second, fiscal policy.
NZ First are more cautious on the degree of public expenditure, although they share Labour's interventionist tendencies.
Labour leads the expenditure promises, albeit at the cost of the planned July 1997 tax cuts. These are delayed in the aim of reducing pressure on monetary policy.
NZ First favours the second round of tax cuts, but wishes to channel them into a compulsory savings scheme (a tax in other people's dictionary).

Since their compulsory scheme is not a flier, at least at this stage, it is likely a large proportion of the Labour expenditure (in areas such as health and education) would be given the thumbs up. This is evident since both parties suggest slower future government debt repayment.

The toil over tax policies will be difficult. NZ First wants to continue with the status quo, while Labour desires more tax relief to low and middle-income earners, at the expense of higher taxes for the wealthier. The labour market is also a sticking point.

NZ First, or at least its leader, will attempt to dig its heels in, resisting large change to the Employment Contracts Act. Their aim is to introduce a "more reasonable bargaining framework and better personal grievance procedures".
In reality, the employment courts already have these issues in hand. Labour will be aiming for more significant change, promoting collective bargaining and returning unions to the fore.

It is here that the gloves may come off. Where there is agreement is the increase in the minimum wages and plenty of active labour market policies. The bottom line -- wage pressures will increase under this coalition.
The key areas that NZ First will be looking for agreement on will be social policy, labour market initiatives, and taxation.
The first is most compatible with Labour, the other policies straddle the Labour-National divide.

In terms of negotiation, Labour will play the Alliance card to NZ First. Alliance confidence and supply support is necessary to make this coalition operational. If their bluff is not called, the majority of Labour's policies will be adopted.
NZ First, by contrast, can play two cards: the National coalition threat and the independent NZ First card. Both plays put the National coalition in government.
And the winner is? The only clear answer is Aotearoa Legalise Cannabis over McGillicuddy Serious.

To the extent that Seventh Day Adventists could not partake in Saturday's frivolities, then the Christian Coalition may also be in for a positive surprise when special votes are counted. However, the special votes are very unlikely to alter the "balance of responsibility".

Providing comfort to the financial markets (to date) is that the Reserve Bank Act, foreign ownership restrictions, asset buy-backs, and compulsory savings appear missing from both Labour's and National's policy platter.

Meanwhile, the Reserve Bank's inflation battle continues to ensure New Zealand is a high yielding investment destination. This has caught corporate New Zealand somewhat unawares. This group was cautious prior to the election and, to the extent they need to get back into kiwi assets, will provide substantial currency support.
Rather perversely, the currency could rise even more upon the widening of the inflation target.

At present a +/-3 percent TWI comfort zone exists around the RB's desired exchange rate. A widening of the inflation target to -1.0 percent to 3.0 percent takes the comfort zone to +/-4.5 percent. It is unclear whether Labour or NZ First, in their desire to please exporters, are aware of this consequence.
In sum, short-term rates will likely remain in the stable hands of the RB, while the bond market will be driven by offshore flows.
Of course we will find out how well the foreign investors anticipated the hung parliament. The longer the negotiations, the more uncertainty.
So keep those brave pills at hand.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters)
